scores.worst_problem: The last point slide's loop, "Three of the four move," opens a specific promise (which costs you can actually control) that the CTA never pays off — it offers a static cost sheet instead.
scores.fix: Either change the final loop to point directly at the cost sheet (e.g. "See all three side by side") or rewrite the CTA to deliver the levers, i.e. which three of the four costs you can move and by how much.

points.title: Same House, Three Prices
body: A 2,300 square foot house prices very differently in San Antonio, Austin and DFW.
Most people moving here only compare that one number.

points.title: Your Tax Rate Has Layers
body: County, city, school district and sometimes a special district all stack on the same house.
Two identical homes ten minutes apart can sit half a point away from each other.
points.loop: The sky sends its own bill.

points.title: Hail Has A Price Tag
body: North of Dallas sits in one of the worst hail corridors in the country.
The same house insured in San Antonio quotes like a different property.

points.title: Miles Are Not Minutes
body: Twelve miles in Austin at five o'clock loses to thirty in San Antonio most days.
Toll roads across DFW and Austin bill you quietly, every single workday.
points.loop: Ninety days a year cost extra.

points.title: August Runs The House
body: Roughly ninety days of triple digit heat every year.
Your electric meter, your lawn watering and your weekend plans all reroute around it.

points.title: Where The $9,000 Sits
body: Taxes, insurance, tolls and summer utilities. Four lines, nothing else.
That is the whole gap between the three transplants. Same salary, same square footage, nine grand a year apart.

linkedinCaption:
Three people took the same salary to three different Texas metros last year. Same square footage, roughly the same purchase price. Their annual cost of living came out about $9,000 apart.

The gap was not the house. It was four lines: property tax layers, insurance, tolls and summer utilities.

Tax rates stack by county, city, school district and sometimes a special district. Two identical homes ten minutes apart can sit half a point away from each other. North of Dallas quotes very differently on insurance than San Antonio because of hail. Commute miles bill differently than commute minutes. And ninety days of triple digit heat reshapes a utility budget.

Relocation clients rarely see these numbers until closing.

What do you think buyers should be shown first when comparing metros?
